title: Sudden surge - cold-cache profiles (personal lab notes)
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal log of experiments that simulate sudden traffic surges when KV/prefix cache is cold. Trying to reproduce real-app pattern where an unprimed model shard receives a short spike and we see p99 blowups even though p50 stays fine. Goal is to capture a repeatable profile, note mitigations to test (prefill, staggered priming, limited concurrency warm slots), and surface candidate config deltas for runtime team follow-up.

Test bed (local-ish cluster):
- Runtime build: runtime-2025.10-e2 (quantized float16 path)
- Model: opensource-7b-variant-v3 (seq 1024 baseline)
- Hardware: 4x A100-40GB (local dev pool), pinned to single shard for target tests
- Ingress front: artifical load generator (kendra-loadgen v0.9) that supports step/spike patterns and arrival jitter
- Instrumentation: per-request trace id, latency histogram (hdr), KV cache hit/miss counters, kernel time breakdown (ATTN vs MATMUL), GPU occupancy sampling
- Baseline warm state: warm-cache (run 30 sequential warmup requests) 

Experiment matrix (summary):
- A: Cold-cache single-shot: start from idle (no KV entries), 200 concurrent arrivals over 5s ramp, 1k token tasks, measure p50/p95/p99 over 1 minute window
- B: Cold-cache staged ramp: same concurrency but arrivals split into 4 waves (50 each) spaced by 2s
- C: Partial prefill: prefill top-K prefixes (20%) then same spike as A
- D: Warm fallback policy: allow fallback to smaller model variant if latency > 1s observed per-request (simulated fallback)
- E: Throttled admission: gate that only allows 40 active inference tokens concurrently, queue rest (backpressure behavior)

Raw observations (not cleaned):
- A (Cold single-shot): p50 ~ 180ms, p95 ~ 420ms, p99 ~ 1.9s, max 3.6s. KV cache miss rate ~ 92% first 30s. GPU occupancy: saw 18-40% transient (lots of kernel re-inits).
- B (Staged waves): p50 ~ 190ms, p95 ~ 340ms, p99 ~ 760ms, max 1.2s. Miss rate initial wave 95% then drops to 45% by wave 3. GPU occupancy steadier 60-80% during waves.
- C (Partial prefill): p50 ~ 170ms, p95 ~ 300ms, p99 ~ 620ms, max 900ms. Miss rate ~ 48% overall.
- D (Warm fallback): p50 ~ 210ms (mix of variants), p95 ~ 380ms, p99 ~ 740ms. User-level quality tradeoffs obvious but p99 wins versus A.
- E (Throttled admission): p50 ~ 220ms (queue add), p95 ~ 410ms, p99 ~ 1.1s. Observed queueing reduces GPU kernel churn but adds tail from queuing backlog.

Ascii timeline (A vs B simplified tokening):
Time(s) | A_active | B_active | notes
0       | 0        | 0        | idle
5       | 200      | 50       | A spikes, B wave1
8       | 200      | 100      | B wave2 join
12      | 200      | 150      | warm cache slowly fills for B
20      | 150      | 40       | A still heavy, B done

Kernel breakdown (sample from A, 10s window):
- ATTENTION setup overhead: ~35% of per-request GPU time (realloc + kernel launch)
- KV autoload and decoding: ~20%
- MATMUL execution: ~38%
- Others (postprocess, memcpy): ~7%

Key takeaways: 
1) Cold-cache single-shot (A) is the worst-case for p99. The root causes appear to be: repeated kernel re-initializations (ATTN setup), high KV miss handling overhead, and GPU under-utilization leading to per-request fixed overheads dominating.
2) Staging the arrivals (B) dramatically lowers p99 because it smooths kernel reuse and allows the runtime to amortize ATTENTION setup across nearer-simultaneous requests.
3) Partial prefill (C) is high-leverage: prepopulating hot prefixes (even 20%) cuts p99 roughly 3x compared to pure cold run. Prefill cost is small relative to worst-case tail.
4) Admission control (E) prevents kernel thrash but shifts tail into queueing. For latency-SLO sensitive endpoints, combine admission with prioritization (short requests first) and soft-fail fast paths.
5) Fallback-to-smaller-model (D) can be effective at tail reduction, but needs integration with quality metrics; can't be blanket.

Open hypotheses / next experiments: 
- H1: Lower ATTENTION launch overhead by keeping a warm kernel pool (persistent kernels) — test persistent-kernel toggle on/off.
- H2: Adaptive prefill: track top-k prefixes from recent traffic and prefill proactively per-shard — measure hit-rate improvement and prefill cost.
- H3: Hybrid admission + speculative pre-warm: when an ingress surge is detected, immediately pre-allocate a small warm-slot pool for top 3 shards.
- H4: Measure effect of sequence length variance: repeat A/B/C with 256-token and 2048-token sequences (expect larger seqs amplify MATMUL portion).

Notes on reproducibility and noise: 
- Results vary by +/-10-25% depending on small scheduler differences and GPU occupancy inherent jitter. To reproduce reliably, pin CPU governor to performance, isolate test machines from cloud noisy neighbors, and run 3 repeats per config.
- Attach full hdr histograms (not pasted here) to the Jira ticket INFR-8123 for tracking.

Action items (short):
- [ ] File an infra perf spike ticket to prototype persistent kernel pool (owner: Evan).
- [ ] Build a simple prefill tooling prototype that takes top-K prefixes from a sample trace and writes to KV (owner: Maya).
- [ ] Add staged-arrival mode to kendra-loadgen and wire as a canary test in perf CI (owner: me - Kendra).
- [ ] Run sequence-length matrix and drop results into the shared bench board (owner: Liam).

Quick raw recommendation for product/console:
- Expose an "aggressive prefill" toggle for Dedicated customers that will run low-cost prefill jobs on low-utilization windows; surface expected cost vs tail-latency benefit in Console.

Random scribbles: 
- Observed one weird run where p99 spiked to 5.2s while p95 stayed 350ms — traced to sudden OOM eviction on one GPU leading to full reallocation cascade. Need to add eviction tracing.
- Consider sampling logs for prefix token histograms to drive prefill heuristics (hot-100 per-customer rolling window).

References (quick):
- Related user doc: users/arrival-pattern-classifier-benchmark-log-sylvie.json (see arrival patterns)
- Git PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2145 (kernel launch refactor)
summary: Personal lab log exploring sudden surge behavior with cold KV caches. Found staging arrivals and partial prefill reduce p99 significantly; suggested experiments and infra action items.
